title: Canvas UI Ships 35 HTML-in-Canvas Components That Run WebGL and WebGPU Effects Over Live DOM
gist: Canvas UI, an open source library from React Bits creator David Haz, is the first component library built on Chrome's experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, applying WebGL/WebGPU shader effects to live, accessible DOM. Its reach is gated by Chrome-only support (flag or origin trial for Chrome 148-150), with Safari and Firefox not implementing the feature.

insights.claim: Canvas UI launched as the first component library built on Chrome's experimental HTML-in-Canvas API, shipping 35 GPU effects (fluid, fire, glass lenses, ASCII filters, VHS grain, particle reveals) that run over real, interactive page content.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A new browser capability is spawning its first framework ecosystem; watch whether rich GPU UI becomes a Chrome-differentiated web feature.
insights.locator: Canvas UI, an open source component library

insights.claim: Canvas UI lays out live DOM inside a canvas, captures it with drawElementImage, uploads it as a texture and distorts it in a shader, so text stays selectable, links stay clickable and content stays in the accessibility tree.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Removes the historical accessibility/interactivity penalty of canvas-based UI, which widens the addressable use cases for GPU-rendered web effects.
insights.quote: Text stays selectable, links stay clickable, and the content stays in the accessibility tree.
insights.locator: Rather than painting a dead bitmap

insights.claim: Canvas UI is the only option that uses the page itself as shader input, unlike Paper Shaders (zero-dependency canvas shaders that sit behind or around content) or React Bits (which animates DOM directly).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Differentiation comes entirely from dependence on a single-vendor browser feature, which is both its moat and its adoption risk.
insights.locator: Paper Shaders offers zero-dependency canvas shaders

insights.claim: The full Canvas UI experience requires Chrome with the canvas-draw-element flag or an origin trial token that runs from Chrome 148 through 150 and is bound to a single domain; elsewhere effects fall back to a plain GPU overlay or unchanged content.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Production use is constrained to a time-limited trial window; track whether the API ships to stable Chrome after version 150.

insights.claim: Safari and Firefox do not implement HTML-in-Canvas, prompting Hacker News concerns about Google 'Embrace, Extend, Extinguish', though a rebuttal noted recent WHATWG issue comments come from Jake Archibald (Mozilla) and Anne van Kesteren (Apple), suggesting it is not a unilateral Google project.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Cross-vendor engagement in WHATWG is the leading indicator for whether the feature becomes a web standard rather than a Chrome-only capability.
insights.quote: This isn't a unilateral Google project.

insights.claim: Accessibility questions in the WICG HTML-in-Canvas explainer remain open, including how drawable subtrees without updated geometry are exposed.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Unresolved accessibility semantics could delay standardization or restrict use in regulated/enterprise sites.
insights.locator: Accessibility discussion in the WICG explainer

insights.claim: Canvas UI is distributed as source through a shadcn-compatible registry rather than as a package, so upgrades mean re-running the install command and reconciling local edits.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Copy-in source distribution is becoming a standard front-end delivery model, trading easy upgrades for local ownership.
insights.locator: Because code is copied into the repository

insights.claim: Canvas UI's registry is MCP-ready, letting AI assistants browse and install components through the shadcn MCP server.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Component libraries are optimizing for agent-driven installation, a distribution channel shift worth tracking in dev tooling.
insights.locator: Licensing is MIT plus the Commons Clause

insights.claim: Canvas UI is licensed MIT plus the Commons Clause, allowing commercial use but prohibiting resale of the components, and its repository has passed 4,600 stars.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Commons Clause signals intent to prevent third-party monetization of the components; traction measured at 4,600+ stars.
insights.locator: Licensing is MIT plus the Commons Clause

insights.claim: Every Canvas UI effect has both a WebGL (GLSL) build and a WebGPU (WGSL via vgpu) build, with wrappers for React, Solid, Preact, Vue, Svelte and vanilla TypeScript; switching renderers mostly means swapping in the -webgpu registry item.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Dual-renderer support hedges against uneven WebGPU adoption across browsers.

insights.claim: shadcn called Canvas UI one of the most impressive registries they have seen, and the Chrome for Developers account welcomed html-in-canvas empowering new frameworks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Google's developer relations is actively promoting ecosystem use of the API, supporting the case it moves toward stable release.
insights.locator: shadcn called it one of the most impressive registries

insights.claim: Flavio Copes praised Canvas UI's engineering hygiene (IntersectionObserver pauses off-screen loops, prefers-reduced-motion is honoured, GPU resources are released on unmount) but advised using one strong effect rather than six and avoiding dashboards, checkout flows and documentation sites.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Suggests the realistic market is marketing/landing pages and creative sites, not transactional or enterprise UI.
insights.quote: use one strong effect rather than six
insights.locator: Writing a detailed teardown, Flavio Copes
